::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- write a function with arguments, default values and a clear return value;
- return several results at once in a named list;
- check inputs with `stopifnot()` and `stop()` and write informative error messages;
- explain where R looks for a variable (**lexical scoping**) and why functions do not change your global variables;
- use anonymous functions `\(x)` and decide *when* a piece of code deserves to become a function.
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source(here::here("_common.R"))
```

```{r}
#| label: packages
library(dplyr)
```

## 1. Why write functions?

Suppose you want to rescale three measurements of the penguins so that each one runs from 0 (smallest bird) to 1 (largest bird). A first attempt usually looks like this:

```{r}
#| label: copy-paste
peng <- penguins[, c("bill_len", "bill_dep", "flipper_len")]

peng$bill_len_01 <- (peng$bill_len - min(peng$bill_len, na.rm = TRUE)) /
  (max(peng$bill_len, na.rm = TRUE) - min(peng$bill_len, na.rm = TRUE))
peng$bill_dep_01 <- (peng$bill_dep - min(peng$bill_dep, na.rm = TRUE)) /
  (max(peng$bill_dep, na.rm = TRUE) - min(peng$bill_len, na.rm = TRUE))
```

Look closely at the second line: the last `min()` uses `bill_len` instead of `bill_dep`. This copy-paste mistake gives wrong numbers **without any error or warning**:

```{r}
#| label: copy-paste-check
range(peng$bill_dep_01, na.rm = TRUE)   # should be 0 and 1!
```

A **function** is a named, reusable piece of code. Writing the logic *once* inside a function has three advantages:

1. **Fewer mistakes** — there is only one place where the formula is written.
2. **Easier changes** — fix or improve the function and every use benefits.
3. **Readable code** — `rescale01(x)` says *what* you are doing; the formula only says *how*.

## 2. Functions you already use

You have been calling functions since the first lesson: `mean()`, `sum()`, `c()`. A function call has the form `name(argument1, argument2, ...)`. Arguments can be given **by position** or **by name**, and many have **default values**.

| Type | Examples |
|---|---|
| Maths | `abs(x)`, `sqrt(x)`, `exp(x)`, `log(x)` (natural log), `log(x, base = 10)`, `factorial(x)` |
| Statistics | `mean(x)`, `median(x)`, `var(x)`, `sd(x)`, `quantile(x)`, `summary(x)`, `scale(x)` (z-scores) |
| Structure | `length(x)`, `nrow(df)`, `ncol(df)`, `dim(m)` |

```{r}
#| label: builtin
x <- c(-2, 0, 3)
abs(x)
log(100, base = 10)
quantile(cars$speed)
```

### `length()` depends on the object

`length()` counts **elements**. What counts as an element depends on the type of object, and this regularly surprises people:

```{r}
#| label: length
m <- matrix(1:12, nrow = 3, ncol = 4)
length(m)       # a matrix is a vector with dimensions: 3 * 4 = 12
length(cars)    # a data frame is a list of columns: number of columns
nrow(cars)      # number of rows: use nrow() for data frames
length(cars$speed)
```

For a **matrix**, `length()` returns the total number of cells ($n \times m$), not the number of columns. For a **data frame**, it returns the number of columns, because a data frame is a list of columns (see [Lists](../01-foundations/07-lists.qmd)). To avoid ambiguity, use `nrow()`, `ncol()` and `dim()`.

### `diff()`: a function with a useful default

`diff()` computes differences between consecutive values. Its argument `lag` has the default `1`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-diff
#| fig-cap: "A random walk (left) and its first differences (right). Differencing removes the trend and leaves the random steps."
set.seed(123)
walk <- cumsum(rnorm(200))
steps <- diff(walk)          # same as diff(walk, lag = 1)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(walk, type = "l", main = "Random walk", xlab = "Time", ylab = "Value")
plot(steps, type = "l", main = "First differences", xlab = "Time",
     ylab = "Difference")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

To see the arguments of any function and their defaults, type `args(diff)` or open the help page with `?diff`.

## 3. Anatomy of a function

You create a function with `function()` and store it in a name with `<-`, exactly like any other object.

```{r}
#| label: anatomy
square <- function(n) {
  n^2
}

square(4)
square(1:5)    # works on whole vectors because ^ is vectorised
```

Every function has three parts:

| Part | In `square` | How to see it |
|---|---|---|
| **Name** | `square` | — |
| **Arguments** (inputs, also called *formals*) | `n` | `formals(square)` |
| **Body** (the code that runs) | `n^2` | `body(square)` |

A function is an ordinary object: you can print it, copy it, and remove it.

```{r}
#| label: rm-function
rm(square)
exists("square")
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Naming functions
Functions *do* things, so give them **verbs** in `snake_case`: `rescale01()`, `split_data()`, `compute_bmi()`. Avoid names that already exist in R, such as `mean`, `c`, `t` or `data`.
:::

## 4. Arguments and default values

### Matching by position or by name

```{r}
#| label: matching
times <- function(x, y) {
  x * y
}

times(2, 4)            # by position: x = 2, y = 4
times(y = 4, x = 2)    # by name: order does not matter
```

A common convention: the first one or two arguments (the *data*) are given by position, all the other ones (the *details*) by name — like `mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)`.

### Default values

A default is used when the caller does not supply that argument.

```{r}
#| label: defaults
power <- function(x, exponent = 2) {
  x^exponent
}

power(3)                 # uses the default exponent = 2
power(3, exponent = 3)   # overrides it
```

Put arguments **without** defaults first (they are required) and arguments **with** defaults after them.

### Passing extra arguments on with `...`

The special argument `...` ("dot-dot-dot") collects any extra arguments and lets you hand them to another function. It is handy for small *wrappers*:

```{r}
#| label: dots
mean_sd <- function(x, ...) {
  c(mean = mean(x, ...), sd = sd(x, ...))
}

mean_sd(penguins$body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)   # na.rm travels through ...
```

Use `...` sparingly: a misspelled argument (e.g. `na.mr = TRUE`) is silently swallowed by `...` instead of producing an error.

## 5. Return values

### The last expression is returned

An R function returns the value of the **last expression evaluated** in its body. You do not need to write `return()` at the end.

```{r}
#| label: implicit-return
cv <- function(x) {
  s <- sd(x)
  m <- mean(x)
  s / m          # this value is returned
}

cv(cars$speed)
```

### `return()` for an early exit

Use `return()` when you want to **stop early**, typically to handle a special case before the main computation.

```{r}
#| label: early-return
safe_log <- function(x) {
  if (any(x <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)) {
    warning("Non-positive values found; returning NA for them.")
    x[x <= 0] <- NA
  }
  if (all(is.na(x))) {
    return(x)              # nothing left to compute: leave now
  }
  log(x)
}

safe_log(c(1, 10, 100))
```

### Returning several results: use a list

A function returns **one** object. When you need several results, put them into a named list.

```{r}
#| label: list-return
describe <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  list(
    n      = length(x),
    mean   = mean(x),
    sd     = sd(x),
    range  = range(x)
  )
}

res <- describe(penguins$flipper_len)
res$mean
res$range
```

The caller picks the pieces they need with `$`. This is exactly how `t.test()` or `lm()` return their results.

## 6. Checking inputs

A function is used by other people (including you, six months from now). Checking the inputs **at the start** turns a confusing error deep in the code into a clear message.

### `stopifnot()` for quick checks

`stopifnot()` stops with an error if any condition is not `TRUE`. Naming each condition gives a readable message:

```{r}
#| label: stopifnot
#| error: true
cv <- function(x) {
  stopifnot(
    "`x` must be numeric" = is.numeric(x),
    "`x` needs at least two values" = length(x) >= 2
  )
  sd(x) / mean(x)
}

cv(c("a", "b"))
```

### `stop()` for custom messages

When the check needs more explanation, use `if` together with `stop()`. The argument `call. = FALSE` hides the internal function call so that the user sees only your message.

```{r}
#| label: stop
#| error: true
cv <- function(x, na.rm = FALSE) {
  if (!is.numeric(x)) {
    stop("`x` must be numeric, not ", class(x)[1], ".", call. = FALSE)
  }
  if (!na.rm && anyNA(x)) {
    stop("`x` contains missing values; use `na.rm = TRUE`.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  sd(x, na.rm = na.rm) / mean(x, na.rm = na.rm)
}

cv(penguins$body_mass)
cv(penguins$body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
```

A good error message says **what is wrong** and, if possible, **how to fix it**. Use `warning()` instead of `stop()` when the function can still return something sensible (as in `safe_log()` above). Conditions are covered in detail in [Conditionals](15-conditionals.qmd).

## 7. Scoping: where does R look for a variable?

When R meets a name inside a function, it looks for it:

1. first among the function's **own** variables (arguments and objects created in the body: the *local* environment);
2. if not found there, in the environment where the function was **defined** (for us, usually the *global* environment, i.e. your workspace).

This rule is called **lexical scoping**.

```{r}
#| label: scoping-global
y <- 10
add_y <- function(x) {
  x + y          # y is not local, so R uses the global y
}
add_y(5)
```

A local variable **shadows** a global one with the same name, and changes made inside a function stay inside it:

```{r}
#| label: scoping-local
y <- 10
g <- function(x) {
  y <- 100       # a new, local y
  x + y
}
g(5)
y                # the global y is unchanged
```

Every call starts with a fresh local environment, which is destroyed when the function finishes. A function therefore cannot accidentally overwrite your data: if you want to keep a result, **return it** and assign it, e.g. `peng <- add_columns(peng)`.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Avoid relying on global variables
`add_y()` works, but its result depends on whatever `y` happens to be in your workspace. Pass everything a function needs **as an argument**. You may meet the "super-assignment" operator `<<-`, which modifies a variable outside the function: avoid it in everyday analysis code.
:::

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: environments
Each function call creates an **environment**, a set of name–value bindings whose *parent* is the environment where the function was created. Looking up a name walks up this chain of parents: local → defining environment → … → global environment → loaded packages → base. You can inspect it with `environment(add_y)` (the defining environment) and, from inside a function, `environment()` (the current call's environment). This is also why a function created *inside* another function remembers the variables of its parent (a *closure*). See *Advanced R* (2e), chapters 6–7.
:::

## 8. Worked example 1: `rescale01()`

We now turn the copy-pasted code from Section 1 into a function. The formula is

$$
\text{rescale}(x_i) = \frac{x_i - \min(x)}{\max(x) - \min(x)} .
$$

### A tempting but **wrong** version

`range(x)` returns a vector of length 2, `c(min, max)`. A natural idea is to use it directly:

```{r}
#| label: rescale-bug
rescale_wrong <- function(x) {
  rng <- range(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  (x - rng) / (rng[2] - rng[1])      # BUG: subtracts a vector of length 2
}

rescale_wrong(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))
```

The result is wrong and R does **not** complain. `x - rng` *recycles* `rng`: it computes `1 - 1, 2 - 5, 3 - 1, 4 - 5, 5 - 1`, alternating the minimum and the maximum. (When the length of `x` is odd, R gives a warning; when it is even, not even that.)

### The correct version

```{r}
#| label: rescale-ok
# Rescale a numeric vector to the interval [0, 1].
# x:     numeric vector (may contain NA)
# Returns a numeric vector of the same length; NAs stay NA.
rescale01 <- function(x) {
  stopifnot("`x` must be numeric" = is.numeric(x))
  rng <- range(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  width <- rng[2] - rng[1]
  if (!is.finite(width) || width == 0) {
    return(rep(0, length(x)))         # constant or all-NA input
  }
  (x - rng[1]) / width
}

rescale01(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))
rescale01(c(7, 7, 7))
```

Notice the **comments above the function**: what it does, what it expects, what it returns. That is all the documentation a small analysis function needs. (Package authors use the same idea in a structured form, called *roxygen* comments, starting with `#'`.)

Now the three columns can be rescaled with one line, using `across()` from [dplyr](../02-data/09-dplyr-verbs.qmd):

```{r}
#| label: rescale-across
peng_01 <- penguins |>
  select(bill_len, bill_dep, flipper_len) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), rescale01, .names = "{.col}_01"))

peng_01 |>
  select(ends_with("_01")) |>
  summary()
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output
Each rescaled column has `Min.` equal to 0 and `Max.` equal to 1, which is the quick check that the function does what it promises. The `NA's` row shows that missing values were kept as missing, not turned into numbers.
:::

## 9. Worked example 2: a reproducible train/test split

In machine learning you often split a data set into a **training** part (to fit a model) and a **test** part (to evaluate it). We want a function that

- takes a data frame and the proportion of rows for training,
- optionally takes a **seed**, so that the split can be reproduced,
- returns **both** pieces.

```{r}
#| label: split-data
# Randomly split a data frame into a training and a test set.
# df:   a data frame
# prop: proportion of rows in the training set (strictly between 0 and 1)
# seed: optional integer for a reproducible split
# Returns a list with elements `train` and `test`.
split_data <- function(df, prop = 0.8, seed = NULL) {
  stopifnot(
    "`df` must be a data frame" = is.data.frame(df),
    "`prop` must be a single number in (0, 1)" =
      is.numeric(prop) && length(prop) == 1 && prop > 0 && prop < 1
  )
  if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)

  n <- nrow(df)
  idx_train <- sample.int(n, size = floor(prop * n))

  list(
    train = df[idx_train, , drop = FALSE],
    test  = df[-idx_train, , drop = FALSE]
  )
}
```

```{r}
#| label: split-data-use
spl <- split_data(penguins, prop = 0.7, seed = 42)
nrow(spl$train)
nrow(spl$test)
nrow(spl$train) + nrow(spl$test) == nrow(penguins)
```

Running the call again with the same seed gives exactly the same rows:

```{r}
#| label: split-data-repro
spl2 <- split_data(penguins, prop = 0.7, seed = 42)
identical(spl$train, spl2$train)
```

The function uses everything we have seen: defaults (`prop = 0.8`, `seed = NULL`), input checks, an `if` that runs only when a seed is given, and a list as return value. In [the ML workflow lesson](../10-ml/44-ml-workflow.qmd) you will use `rsample::initial_split()`, which does the same job with more options (for example, stratification).

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: `set.seed()` inside a function
Calling `set.seed()` inside a function changes the random-number state of your **whole session**, not just of the function. That is acceptable for a teaching example, but in production code it is often better to leave seeding to the caller (call `set.seed()` once at the top of the script) or to restore the previous state with `withr::with_seed()`.
:::

## 10. Anonymous functions

Sometimes you need a tiny function only once, typically as an argument to another function. You do not need to give it a name: write it **anonymously**. Since R 4.1, `\(x)` is a short form of `function(x)`.

```{r}
#| label: anonymous
sapply(1:5, \(x) x^2 + 1)

# the same, with the long form
sapply(1:5, function(x) x^2 + 1)
```

Anonymous functions are everywhere in modern R: in `across()`, in the apply family and in `purrr::map()` (see [Iteration](17-iteration.qmd)).

```{r}
#| label: anonymous-across
penguins |>
  summarise(across(
    c(bill_len, body_mass),
    \(v) round(mean(v, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
  ))
```

If an anonymous function grows beyond one line, give it a name.

## 11. When should you write a function?

A useful guideline is the **rule of three**: *once you have copied and pasted the same block of code twice (so it appears three times), turn it into a function.*

Other good signs that a function would help:

- you find yourself changing the same number or name in several places;
- a block of code does one clear job that you can name with a verb;
- you want to test a piece of logic on small, hand-made inputs (like `rescale01(c(1, 2, 3))`).

Keep functions **small and focused**: one function, one job. A 200-line function is as hard to read as 200 lines of script.

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **Using a vector where a single value is meant.** `x - range(x)` recycles silently and gives wrong numbers (Section 8). Index explicitly: `rng[1]`, `rng[2]`.
2. **Forgetting to assign the result.** `rescale01(x)` prints the result but does not change `x`. Write `x01 <- rescale01(x)`.
3. **Depending on global variables.** If a function uses a variable that is not an argument, its result changes when your workspace changes. Pass it as an argument.
4. **Putting `print()` instead of returning.** A function that only prints cannot be used in further computations. Return the value; let the caller print it.
5. **Vague error messages.** `stop("error")` helps no one. Say what was expected and what was received.
6. **Misspelled argument names swallowed by `...`.** `mean_sd(x, na.mr = TRUE)` does not remove `NA`s. Double-check argument names.
:::

## 12. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. What does `f(3)` return, and what is the value of `z` afterwards?

```r
z <- 1
f <- function(x) {
  z <- x * 2
  z + 1
}
```

`f(3)` returns `7` (the last expression, `6 + 1`). The global `z` is still `1`: the assignment inside `f` created a *local* `z`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. What is `length(matrix(0, nrow = 4, ncol = 5))`?

`20`. A matrix is a vector with a `dim` attribute, and `length()` counts all its elements. Use `ncol()` for the number of columns.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. When is `return()` useful, given that R returns the last expression anyway?

To **leave the function early**, for example when the input is a special case (empty, constant, all missing) and the main computation should be skipped.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q4. Your function needs to give back a fitted model *and* its test error. How?

Return a named list: `list(model = fit, test_error = err)`. The caller then uses `res$model` and `res$test_error`.
:::

## 13. Exercises

### Interactive (run in your browser)

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 1 — your first function.** Write a function `cv()` that returns the **coefficient of variation** (standard deviation divided by the mean) of a numeric vector, with an argument `na.rm` that defaults to `FALSE` and is passed on to `sd()` and `mean()`. Use it on `penguins$body_mass`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_14_1
cv <- function(x, na.rm = ______) {
  sd(x, na.rm = ______) / mean(x, na.rm = ______)
}
cv(penguins$body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_14_1"}
The default is `FALSE`; inside the body, pass the *argument* `na.rm` (not the value `TRUE`) to both functions.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_14_1"}
```r
cv <- function(x, na.rm = FALSE) {
  sd(x, na.rm = na.rm) / mean(x, na.rm = na.rm)
}
cv(penguins$body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)   # about 0.19
```
Body mass varies by about 19% around its mean. Without `na.rm = TRUE` the result is `NA`, because two penguins have no recorded mass.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 2 — debug.** This function should rescale a vector to $[0, 1]$, but the output below is clearly wrong (some values are negative and the largest one is not 1). Find and fix the bug.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_14_2
normalize01 <- function(x) {
  rng <- range(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  (x - rng) / (rng[2] - rng[1])
}
out <- normalize01(c(10, 20, 30, 40))
out
range(out)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_14_2"}
`rng` has two elements. Which one should be subtracted from *every* value of `x`?
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_14_2"}
```r
normalize01 <- function(x) {
  rng <- range(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  (x - rng[1]) / (rng[2] - rng[1])
}
normalize01(c(10, 20, 30, 40))   # 0.000 0.333 0.667 1.000
```
`x - rng` recycles the vector `c(10, 40)` along `x`, subtracting the minimum from odd positions and the maximum from even positions. Because `x` has even length, R does not even warn.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — predict the output.** Before running the code, write down what the three lines at the bottom print. Then run it and check.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_14_3
n <- 5
add_n <- function(x, n = 1) {
  n <- n * 10
  x + n
}
add_n(1)
add_n(1, n = 2)
n
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_14_3"}
Inside the function, `n` is the *argument* (default 1), not the global `n`. Assignments inside a function are local.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_14_3"}
`add_n(1)` gives `11` (default `n = 1`, multiplied by 10). `add_n(1, n = 2)` gives `21`. The global `n` is still `5`: the function only changed its local copy.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★★]{.stars} **Exercise 4 — several results and input checks.** Complete `bmi_summary()`: it takes `weight` (kg) and `height` (m), **stops** with an informative message if the two vectors have different lengths or if any height is not positive, and returns a list with the vector of BMI values (`bmi = weight / height^2`) and their mean.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_14_4
bmi_summary <- function(weight, height) {
  stopifnot(
    "`weight` and `height` must have the same length" = ______,
    "all heights must be positive" = ______
  )
  bmi <- weight / height^2
  list(bmi = ______, mean_bmi = ______)
}
res <- bmi_summary(c(60, 75, 90), c(1.65, 1.80, 1.75))
res$mean_bmi
bmi_summary(c(60, 75), c(1.65, 1.80, 1.75))   # should stop with a clear error
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_14_4"}
Use `length(weight) == length(height)` and `all(height > 0)`. The list elements are `bmi` and `mean(bmi)`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_14_4"}
```r
bmi_summary <- function(weight, height) {
  stopifnot(
    "`weight` and `height` must have the same length" =
      length(weight) == length(height),
    "all heights must be positive" = all(height > 0)
  )
  bmi <- weight / height^2
  list(bmi = bmi, mean_bmi = mean(bmi))
}
res <- bmi_summary(c(60, 75, 90), c(1.65, 1.80, 1.75))
res$mean_bmi   # about 24.9
```
The second call stops with *"`weight` and `height` must have the same length"*. Without the check, R would recycle `weight` and return a wrong BMI for the third person, with only a warning.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — extend `split_data()`.** Add an argument `strata` (a column name, default `NULL`). When it is given, split **within each level** of that column, so that, e.g., every penguin species has about 70% of its birds in the training set. Check the result with `table(spl$train$species) / table(penguins$species)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
split_data <- function(df, prop = 0.8, seed = NULL, strata = NULL) {
  stopifnot(is.data.frame(df), prop > 0, prop < 1)
  if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)

  if (is.null(strata)) {
    groups <- list(seq_len(nrow(df)))
  } else {
    stopifnot("`strata` must be a column of `df`" = strata %in% names(df))
    groups <- split(seq_len(nrow(df)), df[[strata]])
  }
  idx_train <- unlist(lapply(groups, \(idx) {
    idx[sample.int(length(idx), size = floor(prop * length(idx)))]
  }))

  list(train = df[idx_train, , drop = FALSE],
       test  = df[-idx_train, , drop = FALSE])
}

spl <- split_data(penguins, prop = 0.7, seed = 1, strata = "species")
table(spl$train$species) / table(penguins$species)   # all close to 0.7
```
We index `idx[sample.int(length(idx), ...)]` instead of `sample(idx, ...)` because `sample()` behaves differently when `idx` has length 1 (it would sample from `1:idx`).
:::
:::

## Summary

| Idea | Code |
|---|---|
| Define a function | `f <- function(x, y = 1) { ... }` |
| Default value | `y = 1` in the argument list |
| Return the last value / leave early | last expression / `return(value)` |
| Several results | `list(a = ..., b = ...)` |
| Check inputs | `stopifnot("message" = condition)`, `stop("...", call. = FALSE)` |
| Pass extra arguments on | `function(x, ...) mean(x, ...)` |
| Anonymous function | `\(x) x^2` |
| Structure of objects | `length()`, `nrow()`, `ncol()`, `dim()` |

- A function has a **name, arguments and a body**; it returns its **last expression**.
- Functions see global variables but **cannot change them**: return results and assign them.
- **Check inputs early** and write error messages that say how to fix the problem.
- Watch out for **silent recycling** when a vector is used where a single number is meant.
- Follow the **rule of three**: copy-pasted twice? Write a function.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
